title: CVE-2026-3784: wrong proxy connection reuse with credentials
excerpt:
Summary

libcurl may reuse an existing HTTP proxy CONNECT tunnel without matching proxy credentials when selecting a reusable connection.
In lib/url.c, url_match_proxy_use() calls proxy_info_matches() (lib/url.c:930-935 → lib/url.c:589-595), and that matcher compares proxy type, host, and port but does not compare proxy username or password.
When a shared connection cache is used (CURLSH + CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT), a transfer using different proxy credentials can reuse a previously authenticated tunnel.
In my reproduction the proxy receives only one CONNECT request with good:good, while a second transfer configured with bad:bad succeeds through the existing tunnel without issuing a new CONNECT.
This was reproduced both with sequential libcurl transfers and with a wrapper/daemon model where multiple clients submit jobs to a process holding the shared connection cache.
Control tests show the issue does not occur when connections are not shared (noshare) or when the destination host differs.

Steps To Reproduce
1. Build the PoC program using libcurl.
2. Start the local proxy reproducer script.
python3 /tmp/run_share_connect_poc.py
3. The script performs two transfers via a proxy.
Transfer 1:
proxy credentials: good:good
Transfer 2:
proxy credentials: bad:bad


MODE noshare
- first request succeeds
- second request fails with proxy authentication error
- proxy observes two CONNECT requests

MODE share
- both requests succeed
- proxy observes only one CONNECT request
- CONNECT uses good:good
- second request (bad:bad) is sent through existing tunnel
Run the wrapper daemon scenario (curl_wrap_daemon.c) to simulate a service using a shared connection pool.

claims.reasoning: The proxy_info_matches function at lines 589-595 explicitly compares only proxytype, port, and host.name. It does not compare the user or passwd fields of the proxy_info struct.

claims.reasoning: At line 934, url_match_proxy_use calls proxy_info_matches(&m->needle->http_proxy, &conn->http_proxy) when the httpproxy bit is set.
The deterministic checks confirm both CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT and CURLSHOPT_SHARE exist in the codebase, which are the mechanisms for shared connection caches.

claims.text: a transfer using different proxy credentials can reuse a previously authenticated tunnel
claims.reasoning: Since url_match_proxy_use uses proxy_info_matches (which lacks credential checks) for HTTP proxy connections, and the shared connection cache (CURLSH + CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT) enables connection reuse across transfers, a transfer with different proxy credentials can reuse a previously authenticated HTTP CONNECT tunnel. Notably, socks_proxy_info_matches (lines 600-616) does compare credentials, showing the pattern exists but is missing for HTTP proxy.

key_reasons: proxy_info_matches() at lib/url.c:589-595 compares only proxytype, port, and host.name — it omits user and passwd fields
url_match_proxy_use() at lib/url.c:934 calls proxy_info_matches for HTTP proxy connections, so credential differences are ignored during connection reuse
socks_proxy_info_matches() at lib/url.c:600-616 explicitly compares user and passwd, demonstrating the intended pattern is missing for HTTP proxy

Shared connection cache (CURLSH + CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT) is a documented feature; when used, this flaw allows a transfer with invalid proxy credentials to reuse a CONNECT tunnel authenticated with different credentials
This is a security issue: it bypasses proxy authentication policy in multi-tenant or shared-pool architectures
reply: Thank you for the detailed report. The code confirms the flaw: proxy_info_matches() (lib/url.c:589-595) compares only proxytype, port, and host for HTTP proxy, while socks_proxy_info_matches() (lib/url.c:600-616) correctly compares user and passwd. When a shared connection cache (CURLSH + CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT) is used, url_match_proxy_use() reuses HTTP CONNECT tunnels without checking credentials. This is a valid security issue allowing proxy authentication bypass. We will work on a fix.
